title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident shows AI-generated impersonation deployed at scale without authentication controls on social media platforms. Criminals used AI to create synthetic videos and images of a real attorney and built hundreds of fake profiles across multiple platforms, directing vulnerable people to fraudulent services. The deployment happened entirely on social platforms where no human verification of identity or credentials occurred before content went live.

The failure mode is impersonation enabled by generative AI. Scammers created deepfakes that looked convincing enough to deceive immigrants seeking legal help, then used the fake profiles to solicit payment for services never actually provided. What would have caught this earlier: identity verification systems on social platforms that confirm whether video creators are who they claim to be, or at minimum review processes for accounts offering professional services in regulated fields.

It is not established what specific AI tools were used, how the scammers obtained training material of the attorney, or what the total financial loss amounts to.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
A South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience says criminals are using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and defraud vulnerable immigrants. Angel Leal discovered that scammers created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles featuring AI-generated images of him offering immigration services he never provides. In the fake videos, the digital version of Leal promises US residency assistance to undocumented immigrants for $2,200. Leal first learned of the scheme when potential clients began calling his office asking about services he never advertised.

The fraud has grown dramatically over recent months, with Leal's office discovering suspicious activity beginning in October. An anti-piracy company hired by Leal's firm has removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scams typically start with social media videos directing viewers to contact a WhatsApp number, where fraudsters send fake contracts and collect money through payment apps like Venmo and Zelle. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to launch an investigation into the scams.
